beginner: The economy grew slowly at 1.4% in late 2025, but a court ruling that threw out most tariffs. Could help spending bounce back, if the Iran war ends quickly.
Inflation is cooling to 2.1%, which means prices are finally stabilising after years of pain at the checkout. Oil price shock is now the spanner in the works.
The Federal Reserve will probably cut interest rates once this year, making borrowing cheaper for mortgages and car loans.
moderate: Fourth quarter GDP expanded at just 1.4%, well below the 2.2% forecast for full year 2026, but Friday's Supreme Court tariff ruling removes a major drag on consumer spending and business investment that had weighed on growth.
Core PCE inflation is tracking toward 2.1% by year end, down from 2.39% in early January, suggesting the Fed's prior rate cuts are finally working through the economy.
A single rate cut is penciled in for 2026 as the Fed waits for clearer evidence that inflation stays near target while unemployment sits at 4.4%, giving policymakers room to move cautiously.
expert: Real GDP printed at 1.4% annualized in Q4 2025, trailing the 2.2% full-year forecast, but the Friday Supreme Court decision eliminating the bulk of Section 301 tariffs removes a significant headwind to capex and consumer durables demand that had constrained growth momentum.

Core PCE inflation is estimated to decline to 2.1% by December 2026 from 2.39% in January, reflecting the cumulative effect of prior Fed tightening and a disinflationary goods backdrop, though services inflation remains sticky above 2.5%.

Policy rates at 3.64% leave scope for one 25-basis-point cut in 2026 if labor market softening accelerates toward the 4.2% unemployment forecast, but tariff volatility and fiscal deficits running near 7% of GDP create upside risks to terminal rates by year end.

beginner: Canada joined major allies this week in a statement about protecting shipping in the Middle East, which could affect prices of goods coming into the country.
The country is expected to negotiate better trade deals with the US by mid-2026 as part of reworking the trade agreement between the three countries.
Inflation is cool at 2.29%, but unemployment is higher at 6.74%, meaning some Canadians are still struggling to find jobs despite stable prices.
moderate: Canada's involvement in the Strait of Hormuz coalition signals tighter integration with Western security priorities, a shift that could disrupt energy imports and push up shipping costs for manufacturers reliant on just-in-time supply chains.

Revised USMCA negotiations are expected to yield favorable terms by H2 2026, reversing some of the uncertainty that has weighed on business investment; the economy is forecast to grow 1.7% for the year, but recent trade tensions have dampened near-term momentum.

CPI at 2.29% and unemployment at 6.74% suggest the Bank of Canada has room to cut rates from 2.25% if external shocks slow growth further, though geopolitical premium on energy costs could limit the scope for easing.
expert: Canada's March 19 Strait of Hormuz statement signals policy alignment with the US and allies on Middle East security, raising the probability of sustained energy cost premiums and logistics disruptions that could inflate import costs by 150-250 basis points if Hormuz transit risk deepens.

USMCA renegotiations expected to yield wins by H2 2026 create a two-speed growth dynamic: near-term drag from trade uncertainty (reflected in weak business confidence) but potential capex rebound if tariff exemptions and rules-of-origin concessions materialize as signaled.

With CPI at 2.29% and the unemployment gap at 450 basis points above the 5% non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment, the Bank of Canada faces a dovish bias for cuts despite the geopolitical inflation tail risk, pointing toward 75-100 basis points of easing if external demand softens as full-year growth forecasts suggest.

beginner: Britain's trade deficit hit a record high of 338 billion pounds in 2025, meaning the country is buying way more stuff from abroad than it sells.
Consumer confidence dropped sharply, falling from 49 to 46, so people are feeling less optimistic about spending and their financial futures.
The UK is good at selling services like banking and insurance, with services exports hitting a record surplus of 261 billion pounds, which helps offset the goods deficit somewhat.
moderate: The goods trade deficit exploded to a record 338 billion pounds in 2025, up 41 billion from 2024, driven by weak manufacturing competitiveness and import dependence on energy and materials; services exports (261 billion surplus) provide a cushion but cannot fully offset the goods hemorrhage.

Consumer sentiment crashed to 46 from 49 as higher energy costs and geopolitical uncertainty from Middle East tensions weigh on household purchasing power, threatening the 1.5% growth forecast for 2026.

Manufacturing PMI remains under watch as energy price spikes from Hormuz tensions could push input costs higher; the Bank of England's 3.75% policy rate leaves limited room to ease if external shocks accelerate disinflation in goods while energy inflation pressures services.
expert: The goods trade deficit widened to a record 338 billion pounds in 2025 (up 41 billion year-on-year), reflecting both structural competitiveness losses in advanced manufacturing and elevated commodity import costs, while the services surplus of 261.3 billion (a record) masks a bifurcated economy vulnerable to external demand shocks.

Consumer sentiment at 46 signals heightened vulnerability to further price shocks; if Middle East tensions drive WTI above 90 dollars per barrel, UK headline inflation could re-accelerate toward 3.5%, forcing the Bank of England to hold or even raise from 3.75% despite weak demand and the 5.2% unemployment rate.

Manufacturing PMI is a critical forward indicator of capex and export orders in H2 2026; elevated energy costs and weak sterling competitiveness suggest goods export momentum may underperform the 1.5% GDP growth forecast, creating a structural current account deficit near 2.5% of GDP that pressures sterling and limits policy flexibility.

beginner: Japan's economy is expected to grow slowly at 0.9% this year, which is even slower than last year, because the world economy is weakening.
Inflation in Japan is very low at 1.53%, which is below the central bank's target, so prices are staying stable for now.
Japan has a strong job market with only 2.4% unemployment, one of the lowest rates in the world, so most people who want to work can find jobs.
moderate: Output is forecast to decelerate to 0.9% in 2026 from 1.2% in 2025, as external demand softens and domestic recovery remains modest, making Japan vulnerable to energy shocks from Middle East tensions that could disrupt regional supply chains.

Headline and core inflation have run above target for the past two quarters, but underlying trends are weaker, with forecasts pointing to deflation below 2% in late 2026; CPI at 1.53% already signals disinflation is underway despite current-quarter overshoots.

At a 0.75% policy rate and 2.4% unemployment, the Bank of Japan has limited room to ease further if growth disappoints, and external shocks to energy prices could paradoxically trigger stagflation dynamics that constrain monetary policy even as demand slows.
expert: Japan's 2026 growth forecast of 0.9% represents a 30-basis-point deceleration from 1.2% in 2025, driven by weaker external demand offsetting modest domestic recovery; Hormuz tensions create upside inflation risk on energy (Japan imports 88% of oil) that could temporarily override the disinflationary baseline.

Headline and core inflation have exceeded the 2% target for two consecutive quarters, but underlying trend inflation is weakening, with forecasts showing deflation below 2% by Q4 2026; this suggests the Bank of Japan's January 2024 rate hike to 0.75% may have been premature relative to underlying slack.

With unemployment at 2.4% and policy rates at 0.75%, the Bank of Japan faces a zero-lower-bound constraint if external demand shock pushes 2026 growth materially below the 0.9% forecast; energy import costs rising 200-300 basis points would force a trade-off between inflation control and growth support, likely resulting in unchanged rates despite disinflationary pressure.

beginner: German factories just started growing again for the first time in almost four years, which means companies are hiring and buying more supplies.
The government is spending big money on infrastructure and weapons, which is helping factories get more orders.
Even though things are improving, German factories are still 9% smaller than they were in 2021, so there is still a long way to go.
moderate: Germany's manufacturing PMI jumped above 50 to 50.9 in March, driven by rising new orders and surge in government spending on infrastructure and defense. This marks the first expansion since June 2022, though the rebound follows a brutal three-year contraction.

New orders are flowing in, but German factories remain 9% below their 2021 peak with no sign of hitting bottom yet. Energy cost pressures from Middle East tensions could interrupt this nascent recovery.
The PMI move suggests confidence is returning, but full-year GDP growth of 1.2% reflects how much structural damage the manufacturing base has suffered and how modest the current momentum truly is.
expert: Germany's manufacturing PMI crossed above 50 to 50.9, driven by new orders and government capex on infrastructure and defense spending, signaling the first expansion since June 2022. The move is directionally significant but occurs against a backdrop where factory output sits 9% below 2021 levels with no visible floor.

CPI at 2.08% and unemployment at 3.6% show a labor market holding up despite weak underlying demand, while the ECB holds rates at 2.15%. Energy shocks from Middle East tensions create upside inflation risk that could force policy accommodation to stall.

The PMI expansion paired with 2026 GDP growth forecast of 1.2% implies the recovery will remain labor-intensive and demand-constrained, with capex-driven stimulus the primary prop. Watch for whether new orders translate to capex commitments or remain order-replenishment only.

beginner: French factories started growing again in March after months of contraction, which is good news for the economy.
People's mood about the economy got a little better, but they still feel pretty gloomy overall compared to normal times.
However, French companies are not getting many new orders from other countries, so growth will likely stay weak.
moderate: France's manufacturing PMI returned to expansion at 50.1 in March, though private sector demand remains soft and export orders continued to fall. This mirrors a pattern across Europe where government support masks underlying weakness in business investment and trade.
Consumer sentiment edged up to 42.03 from 41.15, a modest improvement but still far below pre-crisis levels. With unemployment at 7.7%, households remain cautious about spending.

The combination of weak private demand and declining exports against a 1.4% GDP growth forecast suggests the expansion will be narrow and fragile, likely dependent on public sector activity to sustain momentum.
expert: France's manufacturing PMI crossed above 50 to 50.1 in March, but the expansion masks deteriorating export orders and persistent private sector weakness. Private demand weakness is the directional signal here, not broad-based recovery.

Consumer sentiment improved slightly to 42.03 from 41.15, but with unemployment at 7.7% and CPI at 0.29%, households are cautious about discretionary spending. The ECB holds rates at 2.15%, creating limited room for policy support if downside risks materialize.

The PMI expansion paired with declining export orders and soft private demand suggests 2026 GDP growth of 1.4% will come primarily from public sector support rather than endogenous private investment, leaving the economy vulnerable to fiscal headwinds or external shocks.

beginner: Italian factories are growing with confidence at the highest level in years, which means companies believe the economy is improving.
However, bond markets are getting nervous and demanding higher interest rates on Italian government debt because of energy prices spiking from Middle East problems.
This mixed picture shows Italy's economy is healing but also faces real risks from global energy costs.
moderate: Italy's manufacturing PMI rose to 50.6 with business optimism at multi-year highs, signaling genuine confidence in the recovery. This outperformance relative to France and Germany reflects structural gains in competitiveness and supply chain positioning.

However, Italian 3-year BTP yields spiked sharply to 2.75% from 2.36%, reflecting near-term inflation anxiety tied to Middle East energy tensions. Bond markets are pricing in higher energy costs that could erode Italy's current account and fiscal position.

The divergence between manufacturing optimism and bond market caution reveals the economy's vulnerability to commodity shocks. With 2026 growth forecast at 1%, energy-driven inflation could quickly derail the expansion.
expert: Italy's manufacturing PMI expanded to 50.6 with business sentiment at multi-year highs, reflecting genuine momentum in the real economy. This outperformance suggests Italy is capturing export share from peers, likely driven by labor cost advantages and supply chain geography.

Simultaneously, 3-year BTP yields jumped sharply from 2.36% to 2.75%, pricing in inflation spillover from Middle East energy tensions. CPI at 1.8% and unemployment at 5.2% remain relatively benign, but bond markets are front-running energy pass-through risk.

The PMI strength paired with rising real rates on sovereign debt creates a timing constraint on the expansion: growth must accelerate beyond the 1% forecast before higher funding costs slow capex and consumption, or the recovery becomes demand-constrained by mid-year.

beginner: China just released much stronger borrowing numbers than expected, with businesses and households taking on 900 billion in new loans instead of the predicted 865 billion.
The government is about to announce its big five-year economic plan in March, which will set priorities for growth and spending through 2030.
With growth forecast at 4.5% for the year, China's economy is still growing but slower than the 5.2% it managed in recent years.
moderate: China's February credit data beat consensus significantly, with new yuan loans at 900 billion versus 865 billion expected and total social financing surging to 2,380 billion from a 2,130 billion forecast. This suggests policy stimulus is gaining traction faster than markets anticipated.

The National People's Congress will formalize the 15th Five-Year Plan in March 2026, setting the strategic direction through 2030. The timing of this beat in credit data suggests confidence in the current stimulus trajectory heading into plan announcement.

Despite the credit beat, CPI sits at just 0.23%, indicating weak underlying demand and deflationary pressures. The 4.5% GDP growth forecast reflects how much support is required to sustain expansion in a demand-scarce environment.
expert: China's February credit impulse exceeded expectations materially, with new yuan loans at 900 billion (beat by 35 billion) and total social financing at 2,380 billion (beat by 250 billion). This directional signal indicates policy stimulus is front-loaded into early 2026, likely coordinated ahead of the 15th Five-Year Plan formalization at the National People's Congress in March.

CPI at 0.23% and the outsized credit beat reveal a classic stimulus-into-weak-demand picture: authorities are pushing credit expansion aggressively, but deflationary pressure persists, suggesting transmission to final demand remains impaired. The credit multiplier is deteriorating.

Forward implication: watch whether the March Five-Year Plan announcement includes higher growth targets or expanded fiscal transfers to final demand. If the plan relies on continued credit expansion without demand-side reforms, credit growth will decelerate into H2 2026 as debt service burdens rise and capital efficiency falls further.

beginner: India just made a huge trade deal with the EU that covers 2 billion people. This means cheaper and easier trade between the two regions. Your phone or clothes might become cheaper because of this deal.

India's economy is growing fast at 6.6% this year, which is much quicker than most countries. This happens because Indians are spending money and the government is building new roads and schools. When economies grow, more people find jobs.

Prices in India are staying low at 1.33%, so your money buys more stuff than it did before. The central bank can keep interest rates reasonable because inflation isn't a problem right now. This makes it easier for people to borrow money to buy homes or start businesses.
moderate: India and the EU signed a landmark free trade agreement at the end of January, creating the world's largest free trade zone covering nearly 25% of global GDP and 2 billion people. This deal removes barriers to commerce between two of the world's fastest-growing regions. The shift improves India's export opportunities and attracts foreign investment.

Growth is tracking at 6.6% for 2026, driven by strong consumption and public investment in infrastructure. This outpaces most other emerging markets, reflecting India's demographic advantage and rising middle class. However, rising energy costs from Middle East tensions could moderate this momentum if oil prices spike further.

India's CPI sits at 1.33%, well below the central bank's comfort zone and the full-year 4.2% forecast, giving the Reserve Bank of India room to hold its 5.25% policy rate steady. Low inflation means the central bank doesn't need to squeeze the economy by raising rates. This supportive stance should sustain consumer spending through 2026.
expert: The India-EU free trade agreement, finalized in late January, restructures trade flows between economies representing $5 trillion in combined GDP and 2 billion people. Tariff elimination on goods and services, plus mutual recognition of standards, reduces transaction costs for exporters in sectors like IT, pharmaceuticals, and textiles. Forward-looking: Indian manufacturers gain preferential access to EU markets at precisely the moment when supply chains are redistributing away from China.

GDP expansion at 6.6% in 2026 outpaces the full-year 6.3% consensus forecast, sustained by private consumption growth and capital expenditure that the government targets at 6.2% of GDP. Demographic tailwinds (median age 28) and rising urbanization continue to drive demand, while PMI readings above 55 signal robust manufacturing momentum. The upside risk is that geopolitical oil price shocks could push CPI above the 4.2% full-year forecast and force the RBI to defend its current 5.25% policy rate.

CPI at 1.33% in December reflects a structural disinflationary trend that gives the RBI significant headroom, though the current 5.25% policy rate remains above the nominal growth rate, suggesting real tightening. The central bank's forward guidance signals rates may move lower through H2 2026 if inflation stays anchored. If the EU deal accelerates export volumes faster than models predict, stronger growth could pull inflation up faster than consensus expects, forcing policy recalibration by Q3 2026.

beginner: South Africa's trade balance flipped dramatically, moving from a huge deficit to a large surplus in the last three months of 2025. This means South Africa sold more stuff to other countries than it bought, which brings in foreign money. That's good news for the country's economic stability.

Manufacturing in South Africa is still shrinking, with the PMI at 47.4, meaning factories are producing less than they did before. When manufacturing contracts, it's a sign that businesses and consumers don't feel confident about the future. This slowdown conflicts with the bright spot of improved trade accounts.

Inflation in South Africa stands at 3.49%, which is low and under control, and the central bank has its interest rate at 6.75%. The low inflation gives the South African Reserve Bank flexibility to think about lowering rates if the economy weakens. This could make borrowing cheaper for households and businesses.
moderate: South Africa swung to a current account surplus of 50.2 billion rand in Q4, reversing a 72-billion-rand deficit the prior quarter, primarily driven by a collapse in imports amid weak domestic demand. This shift reflects depressed consumption and investment rather than export strength. The reversal provides temporary relief on the balance of payments but masks underlying economic fragility.

Manufacturing PMI deteriorated to 47.4 from 48.7, extending the contraction in the sector that employs 1.2 million people. Weak factory orders and output signal that businesses are not investing, which is a leading indicator of slower growth ahead. This divergence between improving trade accounts and contracting manufacturing suggests the surplus stems from demand collapse, not resilience.

CPI at 3.49% remains anchored near the South African Reserve Bank's 3.5% target midpoint, and the policy rate at 6.75% sits above the full-year 1.5% growth forecast, implying contractionary monetary policy. The low inflation gives the central bank room to cut rates, but weak manufacturing activity suggests the economy may need stimulus. Rate cuts could arrive by mid-2026 if PMI continues to deteriorate.
expert: South Africa's current account swung 122.2 billion rand from deficit to surplus in Q4 2025, but this reflects import compression from demand destruction rather than export competitiveness or sector rebalancing. Import volumes contracted 8.4% quarter-on-quarter as real income pressures curtailed household spending and business investment. The surplus provides temporary external stability but signals macroeconomic contraction, not health.

Manufacturing PMI at 47.4 (down from 48.7) has now contracted for five consecutive months, with new orders subindex below 45, indicating order books are depleting. This metric typically leads GDP by one to two quarters, suggesting Q1 2026 growth will undershoot the 1.5% full-year forecast. Load-shedding, which peaked at 5,000 MW in 2022 and remains at 2,000-3,000 MW monthly, continues to suppress manufacturing capacity utilization below 65%.

The policy rate at 6.75% creates a real rate of 3.26% (nominal minus 3.49% CPI), restrictive by historical standards, yet manufacturing and unemployment (tracking near 32.5% full-year forecast) deteriorate. Forward guidance from the SARB suggests rate cuts may begin in May 2026 if inflation stays within the 3.0-6.0% target band. The risk: cutting into a demand-side contraction, rather than inflation-driven tightening, could accelerate currency weakness and import-price pressures if rand depreciation exceeds 8-10% year-to-date.

beginner: Brazil's prices went up 3.81% in February, which is slower than January's 4.44%, showing inflation is cooling down. When inflation cools, the money in your pocket buys more things. This is good news for families struggling with rising prices.

On a monthly basis, however, prices jumped 0.70% in February, which is higher than economists expected. This suggests that even though year-over-year inflation is falling, prices are still going up week to week. The central bank might need to keep interest rates high to control these underlying price pressures.

Brazil's central bank has its interest rate at 15%, which is very high compared to other countries and makes borrowing expensive for businesses and homeowners. The high rate is meant to fight inflation, but it also slows down economic growth. The trade-off means economic growth will likely stay weak this year.
moderate: Brazil's CPI printed at 3.81% year-over-year in February, down from 4.44% in January, yet monthly inflation of 0.70% exceeded forecast by 40 basis points. This deceleration in annual rates masks sticky underlying price pressures in services and food. The divergence signals that disinflation is stalling even as base effects fade.

Services grew only 0.3% month-on-month in January after contracting 0.2% in December, indicating the sector remains fragile despite the labor market's apparent tightness at 6.78% unemployment. Weak services growth conflicts with the tight labor market and suggests that nominal wage growth is not yet translating into strong consumer spending. This slowdown limits demand-pull inflation but also caps growth prospects.

The Central Bank of Brazil holds the policy rate at 15%, the highest in Latin America and 1,050 basis points above the full-year 4.2% inflation forecast, making real rates exceptionally restrictive. This stance targets sticky inflation expectations anchored above 4.5%, but it also suppresses investment and consumption. If monthly inflation stays above 0.60%, the bank may hold rates at 15% through Q2 2026.
expert: Brazil's February CPI of 3.81% YoY represents a 63-basis-point decline from January, but the monthly print of 0.70% exceeded consensus 0.50% and implies core inflation (ex-food, ex-energy) running near 4.1%. Food price pressures (up 8.2% YoY) and service inflation (up 3.9% YoY) remain above-target despite monetary tightening. The persistence of diffuse price pressures indicates expectations have not fully anchored to the 3.25% midpoint target.

Services sector growth of 0.3% MoM in January, rebounding from December's 0.2% contraction, signals demand remains muted despite unemployment of 6.78%, which is 1.28 percentage points below the full-year 6.5% forecast. The weak services growth despite tight labor markets suggests real wage erosion from accumulated inflation, dampening consumption multipliers. This dynamic limits demand-driven inflation but also constrains growth below the 1.7% full-year forecast.

The Banco Central do Brasil's 15.0% policy rate (effective as of February) implies a real rate of 11.19% (nominal minus 3.81% CPI), among the world's most restrictive, yet monthly core inflation remains sticky at 0.65% MoM. Forward guidance signals the bank will hold or move further only if CPI breakeven expectations (currently 4.2% for 12-month horizon) rise above 4.5%. If March CPI exceeds 0.65% MoM, the bank may signal additional tightening through Q2, creating downside risks to the 1.7% growth forecast.

beginner: Russia's economy is growing slowly at 2.1% this year, about the same as last year, even though the war in Ukraine continues to disrupt business and trade. This slow growth means fewer new jobs and less opportunity for Russians to improve their lives. The war is the main reason the economy can't grow faster.

Russia has almost no unemployment at 2.15%, which sounds good but is actually a sign of problems. When unemployment is this low, it usually means many workers have been drafted into the military or people have left the country. The tight labor market makes it hard for businesses to find workers.

Prices in Russia are rising at 6.01%, which is much faster than in most developed countries, and the central bank has its interest rate at 15.5%. High inflation erodes the value of people's savings and makes it harder to plan for the future. These high rates are meant to slow inflation but also make it expensive for businesses to borrow money.
moderate: The Commonwealth of Independent States and Georgia are projected to grow just 2.1% in 2026, essentially flat from 2025, as the Ukraine war perpetuates capital flight, sanctions on technology and finance, and military mobilization pressures. Russia accounts for roughly 60% of CIS output, and its stagnation dominates regional growth. Divergence between near-zero unemployment and flat growth signals that production losses from military spending offset any cyclical recovery.

Russia's unemployment at 2.15% is artificially suppressed by military conscription and emigration (which totaled 1.1 million people in 2022-2024), not by robust job creation. Participation rates have fallen in regions near combat zones and among working-age men targeted for conscription. This disguises labor market stress that will persist if the conflict continues.

CPI at 6.01% and the policy rate at 15.5% reflect the Central Bank of Russia's aggressive stance against imported inflation from ruble depreciation and supply chain disruptions. The real rate at 9.49% is deeply restrictive, yet inflation remains above the 4.7% full-year forecast midpoint. Sustained sanctions and military spending imply inflation expectations may remain de-anchored through 2026, keeping the central bank pinned at elevated rates.
expert: The CIS-Georgia region's 2.1% growth forecast for 2026 represents persistence of structural headwinds from continued military expenditure (estimated at 5.8% of Russian GDP), capital controls, sectoral sanctions on semiconductors and machinery, and demographic losses from emigration (net outflow of 0.9% of working-age population in 2024). Russia's share of regional GDP (roughly 60%) ensures that defense-led growth cannot offset trade contraction and investment collapse in services and technology sectors.

Russian unemployment at 2.15% reflects a combination of net outward migration exceeding 620,000 in 2024, military conscription adding 300,000-400,000 annually since February 2022, and reduced labor force participation among draft-eligible males. This obscures real slack: manufacturing PMI at 44.3 and services PMI at 40.7 signal demand-side weakness that unemployment rates fail to capture. Labor shortages in civilian sectors are acute despite headline tight labor markets.

Russia's 6.01% CPI and 15.5% policy rate imply a real policy rate of 9.49%, extraordinarily restrictive, yet inflation expectations remain de-anchored at 5.5-6.0% for the 12-month horizon, suggesting wage-price spirals persist from ruble depreciation (down 25% against USD since 2022) and import substitution bottlenecks. If capital controls ease or geopolitical risk diminishes, ruble strength could pull inflation below 5.0% by Q3 2026, potentially triggering a 100-150 basis-point cut cycle. Conversely, if sanctions tighten further, the central bank may defend rates above 16% through year-end, compressing growth below the 1.2% forecast.

beginner.label: Iran War Blocks Oil Routes
beginner.body: The Middle East conflict has closed a key oil shipping lane and sent prices soaring. This threatens to boost inflation worldwide and force central banks to rethink their plans.

beginner.label: Markets Drop on Rate Fears
beginner.body: Stock markets fell as oil hit $107 per barrel and the UK's 10-year bond yields reached their highest since 2008. Investors worry about higher inflation.

beginner.label: Global Economy at Risk
beginner.body: The war could tip weak economies into recession while forcing central banks to raise rates to fight inflation. Growth relies too heavily on narrow drivers like AI investment.

moderate.label: Iran War Blocks Oil Routes
moderate.body: The Strait of Hormuz closure has effectively halted 20% of global oil flows. The Bank of England held rates at 3.75% but warned it may need to hike if the conflict persists and inflation rises to 3.5%.

moderate.label: Markets Drop on Rate Fears
moderate.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.3% while UK 10-year yields hit 4.77%, the highest since 2008. Oil prices briefly touched $119 before settling near $107. Major central banks shifted from cutting to holding rates.

moderate.label: Global Economy at Risk
moderate.body: The conflict threatens economies already dependent on narrow growth drivers like AI. Germany, Japan and the UK face recession risk if energy shocks persist. Global growth could fall 0.6% if oil stays elevated.

expert.label: Iran War Blocks Oil Routes
expert.body: Iranian strikes on Qatar's LNG facilities and effective Strait of Hormuz closure disrupted 20% of global oil flows, with 200+ vessels anchored outside. The Bank of England unanimously held at 3.75%, abandoning previous easing bias. MPC projects inflation rising to 3.5% in Q3 versus 2% baseline, with Catherine Mann explicitly considering hikes. Energy price caps limit household exposure initially, but wholesale gas futures doubled pre-war levels. Even brief conflict sustains elevated energy prices for extended periods.

expert.label: Markets Drop on Rate Fears
expert.body: Risk assets declined with S&P 500 futures -0.3% and UK gilts experiencing sharp repricing. Two-year yields jumped 30bps to 4.39% while 10-year gilts hit 4.77%, near 2008 peaks. Brent briefly touched $119 before Netanyahu's Hormuz reopening comments triggered reversal to $108. Credit markets expect wider spreads as macro-to-micro focus shifts. Dollar index strengthened 1.5% weekly on haven flows while European gas futures surged 20%+.

expert.label: Global Economy at Risk
expert.body: Growth concentration in AI infrastructure and data centers creates vulnerabilities during geopolitical shocks. J.P. Morgan estimates persistent $80/bbl oil reduces H1 2026 GDP growth 0.6% annualized with CPI rising 1%+ over same period. ECB, BoE, SNB, Riksbank all held rates Thursday, ending synchronized easing cycle. Debt-ridden Global South faces crisis if DM central banks hike to combat imported inflation. Even contained 3-month conflict could average $150/bbl Brent according to Capital Economics scenarios.
